WORKSHEET · CLASS 28 · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sound Detective Worksheet for Ages 4–5

Detective ear training on paper: a target sound, three pictures — circle every one that starts with it.

Download Worksheet ↓

Teaching tips
THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

This page is the worksheet’s home: see the whole sheet, download it or print it, and pass it on. Solving on screen happens in the class’s own activities on the Learning Path — this page is for the table, the kitchen and the fridge door.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Beginning-sound isolation is THE first-grade readiness skill, and this sheet drills it with a twist: two of three pictures share the target sound, so your child must check every picture, not just find one.

  • Isolating a beginning sound
  • Checking all choices before deciding
  • Pure-sound listening (not letter names)
  • Saying “yes it starts with s / no it starts with h”

On the sheet: Circle every picture that starts with the bubble sound.

WHERE THIS FITS

The class behind it.

This worksheet belongs to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28) on the Age 4 learning path, and the whole phonics collection lives at /worksheets/phonics/. One finished sheet is a full session — download it, print it, and let the fridge door be the gallery.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Sorting by beginning sound means every card gets a listen-and-decide moment. Cutting the cards first adds fine-motor work, and gluing each card in its chest makes the decision permanent and checkable.

  • Sorting by beginning sound
  • s versus m contrast
  • Scissor and glue skills
  • Saying each word before sorting

On the sheet: Cut the cards, say each word, glue it in the right chest.

Rhyming Frog Hop Worksheet for Ages 4–5

Words that rhyme share their ending — hop each frog word to its rhyming partner with a drawn line.

Download Worksheet ↓

Teaching tips
THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

This page is the worksheet’s home: see the whole sheet, download it or print it, and pass it on. Solving on screen happens in the class’s own activities on the Learning Path — this page is for the table, the kitchen and the fridge door.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Rhyme is hearing that two words END the same, and it predicts reading success better than almost anything else on paper. Your child says both words aloud, hears the matching tail, and connects the pair.

  • Hearing rhymes (matching word endings)
  • Saying pairs aloud to check
  • Drawing connecting lines
  • Playing with word sounds

On the sheet: Draw a line from each picture to the picture that rhymes with it.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Blending is the act of squashing separate sounds into one word — the exact skill reading demands. The sheet shows boxes for each sound; saying each sound as its letter is written makes the blending physical.

  • Blending three sounds into a word
  • Writing the letters for each sound
  • Reading back the written word
  • Sound-by-sound patience

On the sheet: Say each sound, write its letter, then read the word.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Writing the missing FIRST sound reverses the usual listening game: your child hears the word, finds its first sound, and writes the letter that carries it. First-letter writing is the starting line of spelling.

  • Identifying a first sound
  • Writing the matching letter
  • Using a letter bank when stuck
  • Saying the completed word to check

On the sheet: Write the missing first letter for each picture word.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Ending sounds are harder than beginning ones — the ear naturally grabs word starts. This sheet deliberately practices the final sound, which is where many children first stumble in spelling.

  • Hearing the ENDING sound of a word
  • Choosing the matching letter
  • Saying the word slowly to catch the last sound
  • Contrasting beginning vs ending

On the sheet: Circle the letter each picture word ends with.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Phoneme counting is the deepest phonemic awareness skill: hearing that cat is THREE sounds even though it is three letters, and that sheep has fewer sounds than letters. Color one circle per sound — hands can hop too.

  • Segmenting words into sounds
  • Counting sounds (not letters!)
  • One-to-one sound-to-circle matching
  • Distinguishing short and long words

On the sheet: Color one circle for every sound in each word.

What your child practices.

Middle vowels are famously the last sounds children hear — this sheet gives them focused practice with the five vowels as a bank. Saying the word stretched out (“cuuuup”) makes the middle sound shout itself.

  • Hearing middle (vowel) sounds
  • Telling a, e, i, o, u apart
  • Writing the heard vowel
  • Checking by re-reading the word

On the sheet: Write the missing middle letter of each word.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Odd-one-out flips the listening task: instead of finding a match, your child must notice the word that BREAKS the pattern. Noticing a broken rule is higher-order listening, and children love catching the trick.

  • Comparing three beginning sounds
  • Spotting the different one
  • Explaining WHY it is odd
  • Confident sound talk

On the sheet: Circle the picture that does not start with the same sound.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Word families (-at: cat, hat, bat / -an: can, fan, pan) teach the big reading idea that words share chunks. Reading each card aloud before sorting means every card gets decoded at least once — that is real reading practice.

  • Recognizing -at and -an endings
  • Reading (or decoding) simple words
  • Sorting by word ending
  • Reading finished lists aloud

On the sheet: Cut the cards, read each one, glue it in the right house.

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

This page is the worksheet’s home: see the whole sheet, download it or print it, and pass it on. Solving on screen happens in the class’s own activities on the Learning Path — this page is for the table, the kitchen and the fridge door.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

The famous trick question: shoe has four LETTERS but two SOUNDS (sh-oe). This sheet teaches children to trust their ears over their eyes — the deepest phonemic awareness there is.

  • Counting phonemes, not letters
  • Knowing two letters can make one sound
  • Careful segmenting
  • Explaining a count

On the sheet: Color one firefly circle for every SOUND in each word.

WHERE THIS FITS

The class behind it.

This worksheet belongs to Phonics & Beginning Sounds (Class 28) on the Age 4 learning path, and the whole phonics collection lives at /worksheets/phonics/. One finished sheet is a full session — download it, print it, and let the fridge door be the gallery.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

A fourth full word-building sheet keeps the complete hear-write-read loop in play with fresh words. By now your child may start writing a letter BEFORE you say its sound — that is the goal: sounds and letters fusing.

  • Independent sound-to-letter writing
  • Three-sound word construction
  • Confident re-reading
  • Spelling-loop fluency

On the sheet: Build each word sound by sound and read it back.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

Ending-sound manipulation completes the manipulation set (first sound with the unicorn, last sound with the mermaid). Your child says the word, swaps the tail sound, and writes what appears — deep phonemic work in a fairy-tale wrapper.

  • Changing the last sound of a word
  • Writing the new word
  • Contrasting old and new words
  • Careful listening to word endings

On the sheet: Switch the last sound and write the new word.

THE WORKSHEET

The full sheet, exactly as it prints.

This page is the worksheet’s home: see the whole sheet, download it or print it, and pass it on. Solving on screen happens in the class’s own activities on the Learning Path — this page is for the table, the kitchen and the fridge door.

ABOUT THIS WORKSHEET

What your child practices.

The path format keeps the target sound in mind across a whole journey — sustained attention plus sound isolation. Circling as you go means the checking is built into the game.

  • Holding one target sound across a task
  • Beginning-sound isolation
  • Visual scanning along a path
  • Self-checking while going

On the sheet: Circle every picture that starts with the s sound.
